title: Structure of a C program — examples
sourceLabel: C Preliminaries: Structure of a C Program — Examples.
objectives: Name the usual parts of a first C file: comments, include, main, declarations, statements, return.
Explain that execution of a hosted program starts at main.
Read a complete tiny program and say what it prints.
Write or complete a standard C program that compiles under the academy judge.
completionCriteria: Trace the greeting program line by line.
Submit a compiling program via the existing judge (Hello, CForge! or add-two-integers).

notes.introduction: A C program is a text file the compiler turns into instructions for the machine from topic 1. First-year programs almost always have one function called main.
notes.beginner: A typical first program has: a comment (notes for humans), #include <stdio.h> (bring in printf/scanf), int main(void) { ... } (the function that runs first), declarations, statements such as printf, and return 0; to tell the system the program finished normally. Braces { } wrap the body of main. Every statement ends with a semicolon.
notes.formal: In a hosted C environment, program startup calls the function main. A translation unit may contain preprocessor directives, declarations, and function definitions. main is commonly declared int main(void) or int main(int argc, char *argv[]). A return from main with value 0 indicates successful termination. Comments are /* ... */ in all standard C, and // ... from C99 onward.

terms.meaning: A line starting with #, such as #include, handled before real compilation.
The function where a usual student program begins running.
A complete action ending with ; such as printf("hi\n");
Leave main and report success to the operating system.
Text the compiler ignores. /* */ works in every standard C. // is standard from C99.

revision: Order: includes → main → declarations → statements → return.
The academy compiles with gcc -std=c11, which is standard C, not a vendor language.
notes.examAnswer: A simple C program contains preprocessor directives, the function main, declarations, statements, and a return. Execution starts at main. Comments document the code. Header stdio.h is included for standard I/O.

body.objectives: You should be able to point at each line of a 10-line program and say why it is there.
body.prerequisiteCheck: You can declare an int and call printf (topic 4). If %d is unclear, go back.
body.introduction: This topic is the first time the pieces sit in one file. The judge you already used for Hello, CForge! compiles exactly this kind of file. The academy never runs GCC inside the Next.js process.
body.analogy: A school essay has a heading, a first paragraph, a body, and an ending. A C file has an include heading, a main paragraph, body statements, and return as the last line of that paragraph. Skip the heading and the reader (the compiler) does not know printf.

rows.role: Ask the compiler for standard I/O.

examples.title: Greeting program (same idea as Hello, CForge!)
steps: printf the exact line required by the exercise.
Compile and run through the academy judge, not on the academy server.

examples.title: Program with a variable
steps: int main(void) { int seats = 51; printf("%d\n", seats); return 0; }
printf uses %d because seats is int.

body.execution: Trace seats program: include processed → main starts → seats created with 51 → printf writes 51\n → return 0 → process ends. If printf is misspelled, the judge reports a compile error and no program runs.

trace.prompt: In the greeting program, which function runs first: printf or main?

predict.prompt: What does printf("Hi\n"); print (two letters and then the cursor moves)?

mistakes: Putting a semicolon after #include <stdio.h> — the # line is not a statement.
Forgetting the closing brace of main.
Writing void main() because an old book did. This academy uses int main(void) and return 0; which matches hosted standard C.
Trying to compile in the Next.js process. Only the judge service may run GCC.

guided.prompt: List the three words in the first line of a typical I/O program: hash-include, the header name, and the punctuation around the header.

independent.prompt: Open the Hello, CForge! studio and submit a complete program. What must the single output line be (punctuation included)?

check.prompt: Where does a usual student program start running?
What integer does this academy use with return to mean success?

body.summary: A first C file is includes, main, declarations, statements, return. Execution starts at main. Comments document. Semicolons end statements. Use the existing Monaco + judge path to run real programs.
revision: Write the skeleton of main from memory.
Mark which lines are directives versus statements.
Submit Hello, CForge! if you have not yet.
